::: notes
Welcome. We spend two halves, with one break between them, on one published claim, taken from a study of what the European Union means to the people of its member states and of whether the economic crisis changed that meaning. In the first half I introduce three kinds of repetition and the SCORE robustness study, in which I was one of the five analysts of this claim, and then the paper and what SCORE found when it checked it. You write down the question that the claim answers, and before the break you reproduce a recorded result. In the second half you become the sixth analyst: you take the analysis apart into its decisions, try alternatives on the slides and send the one that you would defend to the class chart, which we then read against every justifiable analysis of these data.
:::

## What you do not need {#what-you-do-not-need .smaller}

::: {.none}
- No installation: R runs inside these slides, in a tab of your browser, with the data in place
- No git, and no GitHub account
- No OSF account – we read the OSF as readers, without logging in
- Nothing leaves your machine except the one result that you choose to send to the class chart
:::

::: {.small}
**Task 1, now.** R has been loading inside these slides since you opened them, and there is nothing to open. When the cell shows a Run Code button, run it: 270 rows, 27 countries and 10 years mean that the panel is there.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
c(rows = nrow(europeanisation), countries = insight::n_unique(europeanisation$cntry),
  years = insight::n_unique(europeanisation$year))
```

::: notes
Nothing needs installing today. R runs inside these slides, in a tab of your browser, with the data already in place, and we read the OSF as visitors, so that you need neither git nor an account with GitHub or the OSF. The one thing that leaves your machine is the result that you choose to send to the class chart. Task 1 is the cell on this slide. R has been loading since you opened the slides, for longer on a slow connection, and once the cell shows its Run Code button you run it: two hundred and seventy rows, twenty-seven countries and ten years mean that the panel is there. If the button never appears, reload the slides once, then try another browser, and raise your hand if it still fails.
:::
